paras: The lynching of George C. O'Connor was the hanging of the justice of the peace of Antonito, Colorado, by a vigilance committee on the night of July 21, 1881, though some reports place it a day later. The committee accused O'Connor of shielding and leading a gang of robbers, seized him in his saloon and hanged him in an old slaughter-house. Newspapers across the country carried the story as the hanging of a corrupt judge by 'Judge Lynch', most of them repeating the committee's charges as fact.

According to the wire dispatch, Antonito had for several months been infested by a gang of robbers who held up and robbed strangers coming into town. O'Connor, who kept a saloon as well as serving as justice of the peace, was accused of shielding the gang from his bench and of having citizens arrested and fined without provocation. The Las Vegas Daily Gazette's dispatch said all criminals had to be tried before him and were always acquitted, while Der Nordstern added that members of the vigilance committee had themselves been fined in his court.

The dispatch said that on the evening before the hanging O'Connor fell asleep on the train from Alamosa and had the brakeman who woke him arrested. He then went to the Raymond House and covered its proprietor with two revolvers before going home. The next evening, by this account, he rode through town on horseback with a Winchester rifle and two revolvers, "threatening everybody."

The Vigilance Committee then caught him in his saloon and hanged him in an old slaughter-house; Der Nordstern put the hour at 8 p.m. and the place in an old stable building. His body was left hanging overnight with a placard signed by the committee warning that anyone who cut it down before 9 a.m. would suffer a severe penalty, and it was cut down at 9:30 the next morning.

A coroner's jury found that O'Connor "came to his death by hanging, by unknown party or parties." The remaining members of the gang were ordered to leave town within forty-eight hours; Der Nordstern said half a dozen of his friends were advised to move on. The Las Vegas dispatch claimed the committee's action met "the approval of every citizen," and no report of an arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The story moved on the press-association wire within two days, appearing on July 23 in the Chicago Daily Tribune, the New-York Tribune, the Salt Lake Herald, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Daily Los Angeles Herald and the Alexandria Gazette. Headlines framed O'Connor rather than the committee as the lawbreaker: "A Desperado Lynched" in New York, "A Dishonest Justice of the Peace in Colorado Hanged by a Mob" in Chicago and "A Lawless Justice of the Peace Hanged" in Richmond. Later rewrites ran under "They Lynched a 'Squire" and "Got His Deserts," and the South Kentuckian called him simply "a notorious robber," misplacing the town in California.

The Memphis Public Ledger offered the only editorial comment found, calling the hanging "severe, as well as shameful" but predicting that few tears would be shed, since so little was done to check injustice in the petty courts; the Dallas Daily Herald reprinted the paragraph. Through late July and August, country weeklies in Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee, Arkansas, Minnesota and Wisconsin printed shortened versions, some reducing it to a single line about a judge hanged "for letting off too many criminals." No paper printed O'Connor's side, and none mentioned his race.

The date is uncertain: the Chicago and Salt Lake copies of the wire, the Las Vegas dispatch and Der Nordstern place the hanging on Thursday, July 21. The Alexandria Gazette's version, the Cambria Freeman and the New Bloomfield Times instead put it on Friday, July 22, and a shortened wire text says he rode through town "On the 22d." The Las Vegas account, the only one describing the following morning and the inquest, supports the earlier date.

reader.title: Lynching of George C. O'Connor
bases: A vigilance committee seized Antonito's justice of the peace and hanged him without legal process (A2, A5, A10).

O'Connor was hanged by a 'Vigilance Committee' that acted with no legal authority; a coroner's jury found he died by hanging 'by unknown party or parties' (A2, A10). The committee claimed to be punishing his protection of a robber gang and his armed threats (A2, A28).
The press-association wire (A2, A5), a separate Las Vegas dispatch with the placard and inquest (A10) and a German-language account (A28) agree that a vigilance committee hanged O'Connor at Antonito.

accounts.label: Wire report (vigilance committee's case)
accounts.gist: Antonito had been infested by robbers whom O'Connor shielded as justice; after he had a brakeman arrested, threatened the Raymond House proprietor and rode through town armed, the committee caught him in his saloon and hanged him in an old slaughter-house.

accounts.label: Las Vegas dispatch
accounts.gist: He was lynched Thursday night and cut down at 9:30 a.m. with a warning placard signed by the committee; the coroner's jury blamed unknown parties, and the gang was told to leave within 48 hours.

accounts.label: Der Nordstern (German-language)
accounts.gist: Bandits caught in the act were always acquitted before him and vigilance members were fined; the committee obtained what it called proof that he led the band, and hanged him at 8 p.m. on July 21 in an old stable, telling half a dozen friends to leave.

framing.detail: Wire headlines such as 'A Desperado Lynched' and 'A Lawless Justice of the Peace Hanged' presented the committee's charges as fact.
Later rewrites ran under 'Got His Deserts' and 'They Lynched a 'Squire'.
The Memphis Public Ledger called the hanging 'severe, as well as shameful' yet said few tears would be shed, given petty-court injustice; the Dallas Daily Herald reprinted the paragraph.
Short briefs in weeklies reduced the story to one line about a judge hanged for shielding or letting off criminals.

versions.value: Thursday night, July 21 (datelines of July 21 saying 'to-night'; Las Vegas 'Thursday night'; Der Nordstern 21 July, 8 p.m.)
Friday, July 22 (Alexandria Gazette: brakeman 'Thursday evening', hanging 'last night' under a July 23 dateline; Cambria Freeman 'on Friday'; New Bloomfield Times; shortened wire 'On the 22d')

conflicts.note: Most wire copies carry a July 22 dateline with 'to-night', which fits either day. The Las Vegas dispatch, the only one describing the next morning (body cut down, inquest), and the Chicago Tribune dateline support July 21.
Only the German-language account says stable.
The South Kentuckian's place is a misprint of the wire.
